text: You already know file storage as a shared, hierarchical filesystem that multiple machines mount at once over a network protocol. Azure Files is Azure's real product for exactly that: an actual SMB share, and on Linux an NFS share too, hosted inside a storage account, that several virtual machines can mount simultaneously and immediately see the same set of files — no syncing, no delay.

Create a file share with az storage share create, naming the storage account, the share itself, and a quota in GiB that caps how large it's allowed to grow. That solves the one case Blob storage was genuinely never built for: a group of application servers that all need to read and write one shared set of files — uploaded user content, shared configuration, shared logs — at the same time.

A Managed Disk is Azure's block storage product: raw, fixed-size storage attached to exactly one virtual machine and formatted with a filesystem, exactly like plugging a physical hard drive into a single computer. You actually met Managed Disks back in Chapter 3 as a VM's operating system and data disks, without the direct block-storage comparison attached yet.

Create one with az disk create, setting its size in gigabytes and a SKU like Premium_LRS. Put all three side by side now: Blob storage is object storage, accessed over HTTP by API calls, with effectively unlimited scale and many consumers at once. Managed Disks are block storage — fast, low-latency, but attached to only one VM. Azure Files is file storage — a shared filesystem that many VMs mount at the same time.

Same three concepts you already learned generically, now with Azure's actual product names and mechanics attached to each one. The next lesson turns to a different question entirely: how Azure actually keeps your data durable against hardware and datacenter failure, through LRS, ZRS, and GRS replication, plus lifecycle policies that move and delete blobs on their own.
